messages.subject: Density Surface Modelling
parts:
Hi
I was looking for guidance on maximum number of knots to use for covariat=
es for GAM in Distance. I've seen different authors use different degrees=
of fitting for seabirds. As I understand it, it comes down to predictive=
context. If you use just the two covariates lat and lon as a multidimens=
ional smooth, by default Distance will let you have up to 30 'knots' and =
if you accept this you'll generally attain 'better' GCV scores, and the d=
ata will fit your observations better. So if you wanted a map of what you=
saw during survey and you were reasonably happy with your transect desig=
n and spacing, then that would be useful. However if you want a map showi=
ng what could be there if you went out and did the survey again, you're b=
etter off having a lower maximum number of knots (say 6) so it won't fit =
the model too tightly. However this will result in a visual surface which=
doesn't closely match your observations. Is it better in the absence of =
other covariates which may explain the distribution to go for the model t=
hat fits the data better (e.g. more knots) but explain it as just as doin=
g that? Pooling data between surveys may then allude to more general dist=
ributions where the birds like to be, but then we've introduced issues of=
temporal trends, etc... Your expert views appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: Density Surface Modelling
parts:
General thought about curve fitting (whether a density surface,=20
detection function or any other type of curve fitting exercise).

The data to which you are fitting a curve is a 'sample' as distinct from =

a 'population.' Hence it is not appropriate to have a highly flexible=20
surface that can morph to any shape; because you are trying to=20
understand the behaviour of the process that gives rise to the data,=20
rather than the data themselves.

Remember your past understanding of regression. When you have as many=20
coefficients as data points, you fit your points exactly, but the model=20
may predict poorly for situations out of the dataset. Much of what we do =

is intended for prediction purposes, hence over-fitting is something we=20
wish to avoid.

data will fit your observations better. So if you wanted a map of what y=

ign and spacing, then that would be useful. However if you want a map sho=
wing what could be there if you went out and did the survey again, you're=
